title: Asymmetric firewall rule causes control plane TLS resets during Private upgrade
creator: Asha Patel
description: During a scheduled Private deployment upgrade we observed a surge of control-plane TLS handshake failures and API 5xxs for a subset of customer VPCs. The upgrade itself was non-breaking, but an unrelated firewall/SG change applied to the customer's NAT path created an asymmetric return route and blocked ephemeral port replies. This caused TLS session establishment and resumption to frequently fail, producing cascading agent reconnects and degraded API availability for ~47 minutes until a targeted rollback + firewall revert mitigated the issue. This ticket captures the RCA, mitigation steps, and actionable follow-ups to prevent recurrence.

root_cause: A recently applied firewall/security-group rule on an intermediate NAT path restricted source/destination port ranges such that ephemeral reply ports used by control-plane TLS handshakes were blocked on the return path. This created asymmetric routing where inbound SYN/ClientHello packets reached the control plane but return packets were dropped or NAT-mapped differently, causing TLS handshakes to fail and session resumption to break. The upgrade coincided with increased concurrency which amplified the failure surface.
contributing_factors: No automated preflight connectivity check for cross-account firewall/NAT path changes during concurrent upgrade windows
Monitoring aggregated 'connectivity' metrics but lacked per-VPC TLS-handshake-failure breakdown and SNI-level traces
Upgrade flow allowed higher parallelism for agent restarts, increasing number of simultaneous ephemeral ports used
Partner infra applied SG change without validating ephemeral port ranges or performing canary routing verification
mitigations: Immediate: paused rollout and rolled back agent image for affected accounts; coordinated revert of the tighten-firewall rule with partner infra
Short-term: added a canary that exercises a full TLS handshake + session resumption flow across representative NAT paths before scaling restarts
Medium-term: implement preflight network connectivity validation that verifies ephemeral port return path using active probes
Long-term: add a formal pre-upgrade checklist requiring verification of third-party NAT/firewall changes and a signed 'no-impact' confirmation from partner infra

notes: We were fortunate the failure surface was limited to a subset of VPCs with partner NAT changes. Key takeaway: upgrades that increase concurrency interact with third-party networking changes in non-obvious ways; defensive preflight network validation and per-VPC TLS observability are high priority.
